title: Eviction regret analytics and synthetic workload playbook
content:
Purpose and scope
This doc collects a repeatable analysis and workload-generation playbook for 'eviction regret' — cases where an item is evicted and then nearly immediately re-requested, causing extra page-ins, NVMe traffic, and tail-latency amplification. Goal: give on-call/optimization owners a compact recipe to measure regret, reproduce worst-cases in CI/lab, and evaluate mitigations with concrete signals.

Background / motivation
- We've observed intermittent spikes in token-serving tail latency on multi-tenant hosts correlated with increased NVMe read amplification. Many traces show small sequences where lines of KV entries are evicted, then re-populated moments later.
- Hypothesis: a nontrivial fraction of tenant-visible tail latency and bandwidth cost is due to eviction decisions that have high short-term regret under typical conversational reuse patterns (bursty re-requests, short session breaks, prompt-chaining).

Definitions (for consistent instrumentation)
- eviction regret window: 0–15s after eviction (configurable). If a key/page is re-requested within the window, mark as 'regret hit'.
- regret rate: regret hits / total evictions (per-host, per-tenant, per-model routes).
- read amplification: bytes read from NVMe / user-visible served token bytes (measured by IO sampling).
- tail-latency-penalty: 99th latency difference for requests that caused a regret read vs requests that hit resident cache.

Quick instrumentation checklist
- emit per-eviction event with (timestamp, key-id hash mod N, victim-size, reason, tenant-id, model-route).
- emit per-page-in event with correlated eviction id if applicable.
- expose sliding-window regret counters (1m/5m/1h buckets) and histogram of time-to-refetch after eviction.
- correlate with nvme-read-bytes-per-tenant and per-core latency buckets.

Synthetic workload playbook (repro steps)
1) baseline generator: small-step conversational trace replayer. Inputs: seed conversation logs (5k sessions), session inter-arrival distribution, per-turn token length distribution. Replayer respects per-tenant concurrency and uses realistic KV access patterns (prefix reuse + refresh).
2) short-break variant: same as baseline but injects short pauses (2–10s) between bursts to exercise eviction windows.
3) hotkey-surge variant: 1% of keys are hot for a short period (25–60s) with Poisson arrival to emulate viral prompt templates.
4) zipf-plus-temporal: static Zipf popularity overlayed with temporal reuse (Markov-ish) so items have high immediate reuse probability for small windows.
5) synthetic worst-case 'evict-replay': write a driver that warms a host, instrumentally evicts target pages (by triggering synthetic pressure or explicit eviction API), then immediately replays requests for the evicted set to measure pure penalty.

Metrics to capture during runs
- eviction_regret_rate (p95, p99 windows)
- time_to_refetch_histogram (use 10ms buckets up to 30s)
- nvme_read_bytes_per_second and read_ops_per_second
- read_amplification_ratio
- 95/99 token-serving tail latencies (per-route)
- throughput drop (if any) under regret-heavy scenarios
- per-tenant cost delta estimate (extra IO * nvme $/GB)

Representative experiment: 'short-break, medium concurrency'
- Cluster: 4 x A100 hosts (same lab config as prod-sim-4)
- Warm: replay 2k sessions for 20 minutes, steady-state cache occupancy ~72% resident.
- Inject: short-break variant with average session gap 5s, concurrency 80 sessions.
- Observation: regret_rate = 0.18 (18% of evictions are refetched within 15s). NVMe read amplification increased from 1.1 -> 1.95. 99p token tail latency increased by 36% for affected tenant routes.
- Telemetry note: many regret hits were for small victim sizes (single page, ~128KB) but repeated across many items leading to IOPS pressure rather than bandwidth single-shot.

Interpretation guidance
- High regret rate + low victim size -> favors admission or tiny-LRU slab to retain recently evicted small items.
- High regret rate + large victim size -> suggests re-evaluate eviction scoring (size-aware hysteresis) or introduce 'soft-pinning' for items with recent high reuse.
- Low regret rate but high read amplification -> look for prefetch inefficiency or shadow caching causing duplication of page fetches.

Mitigations to try (ranked by deployment risk)
1) conservative grace window: when an item is evicted, keep a 2–8s in-memory 'soft ghost' metadata that allows a fast rehydrate path that avoids full NVMe fetch for tiny items. Low risk, modest memory overhead.
2) tiny-LRU slab for items < 256KB: keeps small things resident more aggressively. Medium-risk due to memory fragmentation; requires eviction debug knobs.
3) eviction hysteresis by time-since-last-access: avoid evicting items that saw heavy recent reuse even if they are cold by frequency. Medium risk but effective for conversational bursts.
4) tenant-aware admission thresholds: prefer higher residency for latency-sensitive tenants (enterprise tiers). Requires per-tenant quotas in cache accounting. Higher product/complexity cost.
5) prefetch-on-evict rollback: if an item is evicted and a refetch is observed within X ms, schedule a background pin for similar keys in same prefix. Higher risk (can increase occupancy) and needs careful throttle.

Experiment matrix to validate mitigations
- Run baseline vs mitigation across three synthetic modes: zipf-plus-temporal, hotkey-surge, evict-replay. Capture regret_rate, read_amplification, 99p latency, and memory occupancy. Repeat with varied eviction thresholds (0.6–0.85 occupancy).
- Compare cost model: estimate NVMe GB saved and extra memory hours, convert to $ delta. Use that to create deployment risk vs ROI table for PM and infra finance.

Data quality pitfalls (watch for these)
- Clock skew between eviction emitter and refetch tracer can misattribute regret; always use host-local monotonic timestamps where possible.
- Sampling tradeoffs: if eviction events sampled at 1/10 it biases regret_rate downward — prefer event surface-level instrumentation for a short collection window.
- Correlation vs causation: high long-term eviction churn can co-occur with unrelated IO storms (backups, GC). Always cross-check nvme queue depth and system cronops.

Notes from quick lab runs (2026-02-20 to 2026-02-25)
- tiny-LRU slab prototype reduced regret_rate from 18% -> 6% in short-break runs, at cost of +4% host memory and slightly worse fragmentation numbers on one host type.
- Grace-window proof-of-concept (4s) gave similar latency improvement but had a small race condition under high parallel eviction; patched by adding a token-based rehydrate lock.
- Tenant-aware admission showed large returns for a single high-priority tenant but increased eviction pressure on lower-priority workloads; suggests coupling with routing-based capacity isolation.

Open questions / next experiments
- Measure microsecond penalty for 'ghost rehydrate' path vs full NVMe page-in for our current driver stack. Quantify break-even size for ghost vs tiny-LRU.
- Characterize worst-case memory fragmentation patterns when tiny-LRU slab is used across mixed model routes.
- Add synthetic 'staggered warmup' scenario: many tenants come online in waves and cause synchronous eviction storms; see how mitigations interact with global autoscaler.

Action items
- [Ethan] finalize tiny-LRU prototype and push benchmark harness (target branch: evict-regret/tiny-lru). Due: 2026-03-07.
- [Priya] add eviction/regret events to the high-cardinality ingestion pipeline and create dashboard panels (tenant view + route view). Due: 2026-03-14.
- [Maya] run cost-model comparison for tiny-LRU vs grace-window and present at performance sync. Due: 2026-03-10.

Appendix: quick commands and configs used in lab
- Workload driver: ./tools/workload-replayer --profile=zipf-temporal --sessions=2000 --concurrency=80 --gap-ms=5000 --output=run-20260220.log
- Eviction instrument config (lab): EVICION_TRACE=1 EVICION_WINDOW_MS=15000 LOG_DEST=lab-metrics:9000
- tiny-LRU config (prototype): cache.tiny_slab.enabled=true cache.tiny_slab.max_bytes=268435456 (256MB) cache.tiny_slab.max_item_size=262144 (256KB)

If you pick one place to start: add the eviction->refetch telemetry and a 5s ghost rehydrate path in lab-hosts; that gives fast turnaround and a measurable ROI number we can show to PM/infra.
